items.quote: Of that one onely chiefe Medicine of the most Ancient Phylosophers.
items.what: that one onely chiefe Medicine of the most Ancient Phylosophers
items.note: The chapter heading names its subject as one single chief medicine and gives it to the most ancient philosophers.

items.quote: This occult Minerva of Phylosophy & this only most precious Jewell is inestimable.
items.note: The margin note at the head of the paragraph gives the subject two further names, an occult Minerva and an only Jewell, and calls it beyond price.

items.quote: I shall here supply what yet pertaineth to that chief and universal Phylosophical Phisick
items.what: that chief and universal Phylosophical Phisick
items.note: The author announces that this place supplies what still belongs to the chief and universal physick; the wording treats it as a thing already spoken of.

items.quote: than which a greater gift of wisdom we never read that divine bounty bestowed on man
items.note: The author holds that no greater gift of wisdom was ever given to man.

items.quote: this most secret Secret of secret Secrets, by which even wonders, yea all things may be done
items.what: this most secret Secret of secret Secrets
items.note: The same thing is named a secret above all secrets, and all things are said to be done by it.

items.quote: the Plannets of inferior Astronomy, whose imperfection and drosse it causeth to vanish by piercing them with its most powerfull impressions
items.note: Planets of a lower astronomy are said to have imperfection and dross that the medicine removes. Interpreted (my inference): the parenthesis that follows speaks of metallick bodies, so these planets seem to stand for metals; the lines given do not say so outright.

items.quote: for it segregateth all extraneous Sulphureity and impure Terrestreity from metallick and Humane bodies
items.note: The reason given: it separates foreign sulphureity and impure earthiness, and does so from both metallic and human bodies.

items.quote: the recovering covering and preserving of the languishing and lost health of the Human body, by its fiery vigour
items.note: A second use: it restores and keeps the health of the human body, by a fiery vigour.

items.quote: to say nothing now of the Magicall and super Celestial use
items.note: The author names a magical and super-celestial use and says he passes it over here.

items.quote: when the Gonetick influence of the beames of the Sun and Moon and the fourth revolution is finisht upon its native Earth
items.note: A condition for that further use: an influence of the beams of Sun and Moon, and a fourth revolution, finished upon its native Earth. The lines given do not explain these words.

items.quote: See the Mo{G214: 1 letter illegible}ade of John Dee of London, and Roger Bacon.
items.name: John Dee of London, and Roger Bacon
items.note: The margin note beside the words on the fourth revolution and native Earth sends the reader to a writing of John Dee of London (its title has an unread letter) and to Roger Bacon.

items.quote: it is endowed absolutly with all created Influentiall power as well in the Elementall world, as in the Celestiall or super celestiall
items.note: The author says it holds all created power of influence in three worlds: elemental, celestial, super-celestial.

items.quote: so doth he usually hide his wonderfull Gifts in wonderfull men
items.note: God is said to hide his wonderful gifts in wonderful men.

items.quote: the consent of all those most learned men who in every age have lived with the greatest admiration and prayse of many, do bear witnesse that this is so
items.note: The author rests the claim on the agreement of learned men of every age, together with all antiquity.

items.quote: besides the ocular inspectation and certification of many of our time
items.note: He adds that many of his own time have seen it with their eyes and certified it.

items.quote: their writings, which are woven of so many Hieroglyphicall, Magicall, and Mathematicall Coverings
items.note: The writings of those learned men are said to be woven of coverings of three kinds: hieroglyphical, magical, mathematical.

items.quote: doth warrant and assure a removall of old age and renewing of youth, perpetuall health, and honest food and rayment
items.note: What the gift is said to assure: old age removed, youth renewed, lasting health, honest food and clothing.

items.quote: to the Pious and holy Phylosophers dignified by Nature and Education
items.note: The assurance is given to pious and holy philosophers, fitted by nature and education.

items.quote: not by usury and fraud, nor cheating wares, nor by oppression of the poor (as most of our rich men are now inriched) but by industry of work and labour of the hands
items.note: The living it gives comes by work of the hands, set against usury, fraud and oppression, by which the author says most rich men of his time grow rich.

items.quote: God forbid therefore, that, sleighting the example of the Ancients, I should either deny such precious Wonders of GOD, and darken the wonderfull powers of Nature
items.note: The author refuses to deny these wonders or to darken the powers of Nature.

items.quote: as if they were but the speculations of idle men, or the empty dreams and fictions of a sottish and doting mind
items.name: the most
items.note: The view of those who revile the art, reported by the author in order to reject it: that it is idle speculation, dream and fiction.

items.quote: whom the Phylosophers call fools
items.name: the Phylosophers
items.note: The name fools for those who revile and do not know is given as the philosophers' word.

items.quote: are not to be admitted to them, those also that dote in their Phantasticall dreams are utterly to be excluded
items.note: Two kinds of people are shut out of what the paragraph calls these divine Banquets: the revilers who do not know, and those who dote in fantastical dreams.

items.quote: Here some are listning, whether trusting to my own ingenuity I dare boast also of the preparation hereof in this place
items.note: The author says some readers wait to hear whether he will here claim the preparation of the medicine.

items.quote: or whether fot ostentation sake I ambitiously arrogate to my selfe the absolute knowledge of this Art
items.note: He names the claim to absolute knowledge of the art as ambition and show; the paragraph goes on to say that is the way of mountebanks.

items.quote: Here I would be taken as an Index, or as one standing at the door to direct others the way they should goe
items.note: In the margin the author says how he wishes to be taken here: as a pointer, or one at the door who shows others the way. The note adds that he may profit others more than himself.

items.quote: because I promised the Courteous Reader a little before, that I would set down at least those things which I had made tryall of
items.note: Points back to an earlier promise in this writing: to set down at least what he himself had tried.

items.quote: I was unwilling in this place openly and most wickedly (which is not the part of a wise man, but of cheaters) to falsifie any thing concerning the undoubted certainty of this matter
items.note: He says he will not falsify anything about this matter, whose certainty he calls undoubted; falsifying is the part of cheaters.

items.quote: this Sacred and Divine Art and Science, not of Sophisters, but Phylosophers
items.what: this Sacred and Divine Art and Science
items.note: The art is named sacred and divine and set apart as that of philosophers, not of sophisters.

items.quote: which the ignorant basely and wretchedly condemn of falshood
items.name: the ignorant
items.note: The charge of falsehood is given as the judgement of the ignorant, reported and rejected.

items.quote: among all Arts, as well Liberall as Mechanick, none aboundeth with so many Imposters as this
items.note: The author grants that no art has as many impostors as this one.

items.quote: to be preferred before all other earthly Sciences by those that are true Physitians
items.note: True physicians should set this art above every other earthly science.

items.quote: for it cannot be that a poor or covetous man should spend his time in the study of Phylosophy
items.note: A condition of the student: neither poor nor covetous, but content with honest food and clothing.

items.quote: pray unto God after the example of Solomon, not for wealth, but wisdome, that he would open to them the Magazine of Divine knowledge
items.note: The true physicians pray for wisdom and not wealth, Solomon being named as the example; what they ask is that God open a store of divine knowledge.

items.quote: who measure their happinesse at least by Heaven, and the Love of God the giver of every good thing
items.note: A further mark of the fit seeker: his happiness is measured by Heaven and the love of God.

items.quote: moved and spurred on to search it out by the love of Secrets and of Nature, according to the Divine Grace
items.note: A further mark: he searches from love of secrets and of Nature, under divine grace.

items.quote: without any foolish hope of gaine or affectation of vaine glory
items.note: A further mark: he wants knowledge, with no hope of gain or of glory.

items.quote: doe in the fear of God refuse no honest, constant and possible labor of the hands
items.note: A further mark: he refuses no honest and steady work of the hands.

items.quote: By Wisdome the heart is made constant.
items.note: A saying set in the margin beside the words on constant labour; the note names no source.

items.quote: that End which belongs to the Master of Nature, to wit, the Praise and Honour of God, and the good of his needy neighbor
items.note: The text says what the end of using these gifts is: the praise and honour of God and the good of the needy neighbour.

items.quote: in a constant Taciturnity, without pride, which provoketh the envy of all men
items.note: The gifts are to be used in constant silence and without pride.

items.quote: They that carry about their Treasure and use it publickly. Job 22.25.
items.name: Job 22.25.
items.note: The margin note at the head of the paragraph speaks of those who carry their treasure about and use it openly, and names a place in Job.

items.quote: among the Children of the golden doctrine (whose gold is the Omnipotent God)
items.note: Stated: the text itself says the gold of this golden doctrine is God, so gold is not meant plainly here.

items.quote: that most rare Good, which is to be prefer'd before all riches, is justly and of right to be searched out for the health sake of men
items.note: By the seekers just described the rare good is rightly sought, and for the sake of men's health.

items.quote: leaving the mettalls to those who with an impious hunger, and a thirsty and insatiable desire of being rich
items.note: Such seekers leave the metals to those driven by the desire of riches.

items.quote: A Phylosopher must covet Nothing but Wisdome, which is conversant about Divine things
items.note: A philosopher may desire wisdom only; the text adds that wisdom has to do with divine things.

items.quote: therefore a true Phylosopher never sought after nor desired riches, but is rather delighted with the Mysteries of Nature
items.note: The true philosopher does not seek riches but delights in the mysteries of Nature.

items.quote: he that is adept or hath attained the same may carry about with him in his purse, not the worth of one Kingdom only, but the wealth almost of the whole World
items.note: The one who has attained is said to carry in his purse nearly the wealth of the whole world. The word adept is set beside 'hath attained the same'.

items.quote: But that gift is acquired, neither by wrath nor forced violence, but either by the immediate inspiration of the most High, or by the expert ocular demonstration of a wise Master in this Art.
items.note: Two ways only to the gift: direct inspiration from God, or being shown it before one's eyes by a wise master.

items.quote: But who among many thousands is it, who while he seeketh this very knowledge by a certaine and subduing judgement and due means
items.note: The author asks who among many thousands of seekers reaches it; the question implies very few.

items.quote: passe thorow the porch and gate of the Heavens into the Oratory or Chappell of Apollo, and get to the top of the mount of Chymistry
items.note: Attaining the knowledge by another's help is put as passing a porch and gate into a chapel of Apollo and climbing a mount of Chymistry: figures of place for reaching the art.

items.quote: except he hat for a long time, and by much experience known him to be singularly eminent in the Feare of god, Holinesse of life, pure and Harpocraticall Faith
items.note: No one would help another in this unless long trial had shown him eminent in fear of God, holy life and a faith called Harpocraticall; the lines given do not say what that word means.

items.quote: But where is that Aegyptian Bird to be found, that we may commend such a Phaenix?
items.note: The margin calls the person so proved an Egyptian bird and a Phaenix, and asks where such a one is found.

items.quote: See Paracel. in his fragments of Physick, which are to be refer'd to the 4 Tome fol. 311.
items.name: Paracel.
items.note: The margin note names a writing of Paracel., with tome and leaf, beside this passage.

items.quote: No man hath entrance hereunto bu{G216: 1 letter illegible} by Divine revelation, or by word of month from h{G217: 1 letter illegible}m that hath the Secret, & teacheth it while he liveth.
items.note: Entrance is by divine revelation or by spoken word from a living holder of the secret. The sentence follows the reference to Paracel.; the note does not show whether the words are his or the author's.

items.quote: There is no perfection of things without the help of Divinity, and its demonstration.
items.note: The note ends by saying nothing is perfected without the help of divinity. Whose words these are is not shown.

items.quote: He that desireth this Art, must not be a slave to other mens judgment, nor live upon their purse, and must retire himselfe
items.note: Three demands on the seeker: his own judgement, his own means, and withdrawal from company.

items.quote: Too much acquantance hinder them / Who labour to find out this Gem.
items.note: Two lines of verse give the reason for withdrawing: much acquaintance hinders the seeker. The thing sought is here called a Gem. The verse carries no name.

items.quote: Praebet amicorum, nil nisi copia damnum.
items.note: A Latin line stands in the margin beside the English verse; the note names no author.

items.quote: the arrogant loquacity, the pertinacious incredulity, the envy and detestable infidelity and an Epicurean indignity, doth hinder and much disturb the effect in any operation
items.note: The faults of a companion (talk, unbelief, envy, faithlessness) are said to hinder the effect of any operation.

items.quote: Reverend antiquity, with one consent acknowledgeth that never any from the first man to the last could find ont the Divine secreu of that Art
items.name: Reverend antiquity
items.note: Given as the agreed word of antiquity: no one ever found the secret of the art; the following words, partly unread, speak of natural wit, reason and experience as the means that fail.

items.quote: it is somthing Divine and hid, and that which is above Reason
items.note: The reason given: the thing is divine, hidden and above reason.

items.quote: those who have labored and toyled to find out this knowledg by dayly reading and comparing of Authors, do witnesse
items.note: The long and fruitless pains of those who sought it by reading and comparing authors are called as witness.

items.quote: the glorious God and most blessed bestower of all graces hath reavealed and made it plaine to his faithfull wise ones
items.note: Against that, God has revealed it and made it plain to his faithful wise ones.

items.quote: Ecclesiastic. 38.
items.name: Ecclesiastic. 38.
items.note: The margin names Ecclesiastic. 38 beside the words on God revealing it to his faithful wise ones.

items.quote: The one only and true way to all Secrets is to have recourse to God the author of all good, according to our Saviours command.
items.note: The margin note at the head of the paragraph says there is one way to all secrets: recourse to God, as the Saviour commands.

items.quote: when men seek the Kingdome of God, and study to finde out the Celestiall Stone in the last place
items.note: The author gives as a cause of failure that men put the seeking of the Kingdom of God, and the study of a stone here called Celestiall, last.

items.quote: there is not one to whom the doors of Nature are unlockt, and that hath the Divine bolt removed
items.note: Among thousands who seek, not one has the doors of Nature unlocked and the divine bolt drawn.

items.quote: who giveth his gifts to whom he will, and withdraweth them from whom be pleaseth
items.note: The cause is placed in the will of God, who gives and withdraws his gifts as he pleases.

items.quote: who knoweth that it is not expedient for all to their salvation, that they should have Honors & riches with their health
items.note: A further reason: God knows that honours and riches together with health do not serve every man's salvation.

items.quote: And though happily some one or other may get the key of the Phylosophicall Garden (as I know some that have)
items.note: The author says he knows some who have got the key of the garden.

items.quote: yet because the Gate was bolted, that is, the Divine Grace and Benediction was denyed and did resist
items.note: Stated: the text itself explains the bolted gate as divine grace and blessing denied.

items.quote: gather those desired fruits of the Hermetick Tree, and eate the most sweet kernells of this mystery
items.note: What such men could not do is put in a figure of gathering the fruit of a tree and eating the kernels of the mystery.

items.quote: having got the most true Phylosophycall Ferment or Leaven (but prepar'd by others) have not been able to improve or multiply it any further by reason of the ignorance of the principle or beginning
items.note: Some impostors of the author's time are said to have held the true ferment or leaven, made by others, and to have failed to improve or multiply it because they did not know its principle or beginning.

items.quote: this most holy science never admitted any such unskilfull Thraso's into its inner rooms
items.note: The science is said to keep such men out of its inner rooms.

items.quote: This is that work that is hid under the robe of the Phylosophicall Virgin, which even one brother would not teach another
items.note: The work is said to be hidden under the robe of the Phylosophicall Virgin, and not taught even from brother to brother.

items.quote: it is to no purpose to tempt an Adept Phylosopher with promises of rewards, favour, or any other kind of respects that can be imagined, to part with it
items.note: No reward or favour will bring an adept philosopher to part with it.

items.quote: which even one brother would not teach another
items.note: Here the work is not taught even to a brother; CH6.12 names the ocular demonstration of a wise master as one of two ways to the gift, and N258 names word of mouth from one who has the secret and teaches it while he lives.

items.quote: This is that Secret laid up and buryed in the most secret Treasury of the Mind and Memory
items.note: The secret is kept in mind and memory.

items.quote: doe study and strive to be harsh and rugged, least they should disclose their more abstruse or dark sence to any, and expose the most noble Gemm of this Science to hogs and swine
items.note: The philosophers the text calls genuine and more occult are said to write harshly and roughly on purpose, so that their dark sense is not disclosed to the unworthy.

items.quote: God would not manifest this knowledg to all, to avoyd offence.
items.note: The margin gives a reason for the hiding: God would not show this knowledge to all.

items.quote: have in a wise and ingenious craft covenanted and sworn they would never write it plainly in any Book
items.note: The philosophers are said to have bound themselves by covenant and oath never to write it plainly in any book.

items.quote: Nor hath any of them who kept this knowledge in the secret of their heart, made it known to any but such who had an understanding allegorically
items.note: It was made known only to those able to understand allegorically.

items.quote: because they are made Lords of Things, they should also have power to dispence or give Names at their pleasure
items.note: The philosophers are said to have the freedom to give names as they please: a warning from the text that the names in their writings are of their own choosing.

items.quote: and cloath their children as they listed
items.note: The naming is put a second time as clothing their children as they liked. Interpreted (my inference): the children are the things the philosophers name; the lines given do not say so.

items.quote: This is not believed, but being proved with the gain of labor, toyl and hazard, it is made plain toward the end which proveth the work.
items.note: The margin says the matter is not believed, but is made plain by labour and hazard, toward the end of the work.

items.quote: On this the hinge of the whole busines turneth, as Gold animated by the Salt of Niture is made the chief subject of the Phylosophers metallick Physicks
items.what: the chief subject of the Phylosophers metallick Physicks
items.note: The margin names what the whole business turns on and gives, as its likeness or instance, Gold animated by the Salt of Niture as the chief subject of the philosophers' metallic physick.

items.quote: Though True Phylosophers exactly & with greatest ingenuity, have mutually ingag'd and set themselves upon one and the same thing
items.note: The true philosophers are all said to be set upon one and the same thing.

items.quote: in their precepts, as in a glasse, it hath been sufficiently made known to men of a wise understanding, who are chosen of God to such mysteries, worthy men, and sworn in this Art
items.note: Their precepts show it, as in a glass, enough for one kind of reader: the wise, chosen of God, worthy and sworn in the art.

items.quote: Neverthelesse religously affirming, that none can attaine the desired end
items.name: True Phylosophers
items.note: What follows on the joining of two things is given as the philosophers' own affirmation: without it no one reaches the desired end.

items.quote: though they sleight all particulars, which naturally doe altogether want the virtue of tincturing, unlesse they proceed from the first fountaine
items.note: Inside that affirmation: things called particulars lack the power of tincturing unless they come from the first fountain.

items.quote: before the fat or blood of the Sun and the Dew of the Lunary, be joyned into one body by the circular wheel of the Elements with the help of Art and Nature in the form of an Hexagon
items.note: The step named as needful: two things, the fat or blood of the Sun and the Dew of the Lunary, joined into one body, by the circular wheel of the Elements, with art and nature, in the form of an Hexagon. The words are covered ones and the lines given do not open them.

items.quote: Read Gen. 1.27, 28. Hermes his Table, Morienes, Alan. Rodargir. Monad. T{G223: 1 letter illegible}evisan. Lull.
items.name: Gen. 1.27, 28. Hermes his Table, Morienes, Alan. Rodargir. Monad. Lull.
items.note: Beside the joining in the form of an Hexagon the margin lists writings and persons to read; one name has an unread letter.

items.quote: which can never be done except the most High God please, who alone of his speciall mercy graciously bestoweth this singular gift of the Holy Spirit
items.note: The joining cannot be done unless God pleases; the gift is called a gift of the Holy Spirit.

items.quote: let that man use what Arts soever he can, yet shall he never get any thing against the Will of God
items.note: Here a man to whom God gives none of his treasures never gets anything, whatever arts he uses; CH6.19 tells of impostors who by unlawful means had got the true ferment, though they could not multiply it.

items.quote: for the Spirit proceedeth from Grace, who inspireth whom he will
items.note: The paragraph closes on grace: the Spirit inspires whom he will.

items.quote: Seeing therefore all mans endeavor is but vaine except God prosper it
items.note: The author's conclusion: human effort is vain unless God prospers it.

items.quote: Levit. 26.20.
items.name: Levit. 26.20.
items.note: The margin names a place in Levit. beside the words on vain endeavour and on God as moderator of the universe.

items.quote: should suffer themselves to be cheated and deceived, with the greedy world by the golden promises of circumforaneous, vitious, and most lying Impostors
items.note: The author wonders that many great men of his age let themselves be cheated by the golden promises of wandering impostors.

items.quote: Great men commit great errours.
items.note: A saying in the margin beside the words on great men who are cheated.

items.name: Psal. 25.14. Prov. 3.32. Wisd. 1.4. Eccl. 43.32, 33.
items.note: The same note lists four places of scripture beside the passage.

items.quote: without the liberall and right noble arts (of which those Phylosophists and Imposters are altogether destitute, having not tasted so much as a drop of the Springs of Nature) no perfect perception of Mysteries can be attained to
items.note: Without the liberal and noble arts no perfect perception of mysteries is reached; the impostors, here also called Phylosophists, are said to lack those arts wholly.

items.quote: Those Gymnosophists with their Fantasticall and Frantick inventions, inrich the eares of credulous men that they may make their pockets poor
items.note: The same deceivers, here called Gymnosophists, fill the ears of the credulous to empty their pockets.

items.quote: whose company we should avoyd even as the most raging torments of hell
items.note: The author's counsel: avoid their company.

items.quote: the Wisdome of the Lord, whose mysterie is onely with them that Fear him
items.note: The mystery of the Lord's wisdom is only with those who fear him; the paragraph goes on to say it does not enter the souls of deceivers.

items.quote: with their guilfull devices of painting white and red, and pargetting womens faces
items.note: The deceivers' devices are named as painting white and red and plastering women's faces. Several defensible readings: (a) plainly, they sell face paints; (b) a figure for a false show of colour laid on the surface, which CH6.25 supports where they find 'only the colour' in place of the Tincture. The lines given do not settle it.

items.quote: Great gaine is the scope of sophisticall craft, because Dust & Ashes is the end of such smock-sellers.
items.note: The margin says gain is the aim of the sophistical craft and dust and ashes its end; it calls its men smock-sellers, a word the lines given do not explain.

items.quote: Thus these men playing away and losing the story of Pandora
items.note: The deceivers' loss is put as playing away and losing the story of Pandora; the lines given do not say what is meant by it.

items.quote: instead of the Tincture they should find only the colour, instead of the Hermetick Stone a pibble or glasse, and instead of great Treasure and riches nothing but coals and ashes
items.name: Alphidius
items.note: Given as what Alphidius foretold for such men: colour for the Tincture, a pebble or glass for the Hermetick Stone, coals and ashes for treasure.

items.quote: Piety is the most necessary key to the knowledge of all Secrets.
items.note: The margin note at the head of the paragraph names piety as the key most needed for knowing any secret.

items.quote: this efficacious transmutatory virtue of these Impostors, which makes wise men fools, strong men weak, rich men poor
items.note: The word for the power of changing is here turned on the impostors: what they change is men, for the worse. The word is not meant plainly in this place.

items.quote: against those sacrilegious souldiers who threatningly and malepertly rush into the Vestry of Phylosophy
items.name: Rodargirus BRITTO SARMATUS
items.note: The margin sends the reader to a verse of Rodargirus BRITTO SARMATUS (the place has unread letters), said to be against those who force their way into the Vestry of Phylosophy.

items.quote: It is not expedient to reveal it to any carnall man, because thou wilt be accuised for making known so great a Secret.
items.note: A warning in the margin against revealing it to a carnal man. The note does not show whose words these are.

items.quote: He that publisheth this Art, let him die an evill death, saith Lully, because it is a secret to be given and revealed by God alone who hath created Nature, and no other
items.name: Lully
items.note: Given as Lully's words: a curse on whoever publishes the art, because the secret is God's alone to reveal.

items.name: Job 34.11. Prov. 24.12. Apoc. 2.23. & 22.12. Es. 3.10, 11 Jer. 17.10. & 32.19. Ezek. 33.20.
items.note: The note ends with a list of places of scripture.

items.quote: the envy of Phylosophers is not against the Children of Art and Science, who seek not their own but Gods glory
items.note: The philosophers' envy, the word used here for their withholding, is not turned against the Children of Art and Science.

items.quote: he that is an Adept and compleat Phylosopher, a keeper of Gods Secrets, and is conformed to the dignification of his work
items.what: an Adept and compleat Phylosopher, a keeper of Gods Secrets
items.note: The adept is set apart as a complete philosopher and a keeper of God's secrets.

items.quote: after he by the Blessing of God hath happily labored like Hermes more then twenty years
items.note: The adept's labour is put at more than twenty years, likened to that of Hermes.

items.quote: to publish to the wicked enemies of the Children of Art and Science, or to such as are unworthy of it, this greatest and richest Terrene Treasure
items.note: The paragraph says the adept would sooner die a hundred deaths than publish this treasure to the wicked or the unworthy.

items.quote: the Perfect Benefit or good gift of GOD, descending from the Father of Lights
items.what: the Perfect Benefit or good gift of GOD
items.note: The treasure is named again as God's perfect gift, come down from the Father of Lights.

items.quote: which Secret would by evill men, with the ruine of the whole world, be abused
items.note: A reason for keeping it: evil men would abuse the secret, to the ruin of the whole world.

items.quote: except he can give a good account of his Stewardship and the Talent committed to him
items.note: The adept holds the secret as a steward and must answer for it at the last judgement, on pain of his soul.

items.quote: the heat of the Centre united to the heat of Sun shall set all corruption of the Elements on fire
items.note: Of the last day the author says the heat of the centre joined with the heat of the Sun shall set the corruption of the elements on fire.

items.quote: when every evill and impure thing shall be cast like lead with the damned into Hell
items.note: Every evil and impure thing is then cast out; the likeness used is lead.

items.quote: with unquenchable brimston like molten glasse, continually burning and never wasting
items.note: The torment is by brimstone, likened to molten glass, that burns without consuming.

items.quote: Apoc. 20.10. The end of the world is by fire.
items.name: Apoc. 20.10.
items.note: The margin names a place in Apoc. and says the world ends by fire.

items.quote: There is a Sea of glass mingled with fire. Apoc. 15.2.
items.name: Apoc. 15.2.
items.note: A second place in Apoc. is named for a sea of glass mingled with fire, beside the paragraph's molten glass.

items.quote: The property of fire is to seperate the impurity of the Elements.
items.note: The margin states a property of fire: it separates the impurity of the elements.

items.quote: Read Isa. Holand in opere minerali. Rom. 8.19, 23.
items.name: Isa. Holand in opere minerali. Rom. 8.19, 23.
items.note: The note sends the reader to a writing of Isa. Holand and names a place in Rom.
